## Purpose {.unnumbered .unlisted}

_Why can a better prediction still produce a worse physical action?_

A learned model can recognize a task correctly and still act too late to stop a moving machine or prevent excessive contact force. Once a command produces motion or heat, replacing the prediction cannot undo the work already delivered. The engineer must therefore connect model quality to the body's limits, the time available to respond, and the evidence supporting the next action. An independent permission path must be able to refuse a proposal and carry out a feasible fallback even when the model stalls. At the causal boundary, where commands become physical work, irreversibility makes these responsibilities part of the system's architecture.

## Artificial Intelligence Beyond Glass {#sec-boundary-beyond-glass}

A warehouse mobile manipulator must collect an object from a conveyor, open a spring-latched cage door, and carry its load through an aisle shared with people. These tasks join abilities often studied separately. The machine must recognize an unfamiliar object, choose a grasp, coordinate its arm and base, and respond when contact or the scene differs from expectation. Learning makes varied behavior possible; engineering must turn that behavior into useful, repeatable physical work.

This book develops the ability to design, teach, integrate, evaluate, and maintain such a machine within justified operating limits. Its recurring warehouse machine is an illustrative engineering design, not a report of a qualified deployment. The same task connects physical budgets, learning experiments, runtime decisions, and evidence for service. When the evidence is incomplete, the engineer must identify what measurement, new experience, or design change would support the next capability.

Consider the base approaching the end of a storage rack while its model processes a camera image. A worker steps into the aisle before the next proposal returns. The computer can still discard that proposal, but the robot has continued moving throughout the calculation. Choosing an action requires reasoning about both the prediction and the physical state in which it will execute.

For an advisory model, an output can be inspected or rejected before another system acts on it. Digital mistakes can still cause harm, and computation itself consumes energy. The distinction is that restoring a software state cannot restore the position of a moving robot or repair an object it has struck. The engineering problem begins with this difference and leads from physical limits to the architecture that checks each proposed action.

The physical plant is the apparatus being controlled, such as the robot's wheeled base or arm. Its state changes while the computer calculates. The model must recognize a useful action, the execution mechanism must judge it while the observation remains relevant, and the body must be able to deliver the admitted motion or a feasible alternative. A stronger prediction alone cannot recover clearance already consumed during computation.

**Moravec's paradox**\index{Moravec's paradox}[^fn-ai-moravec-paradox] [@moravec1988mind] helps explain the interest in learning for physical tasks: sensorimotor skills that people perform with little conscious effort can be difficult to reproduce computationally. Learned models extend the range of scenes and tasks a machine can interpret. Their usefulness creates a further obligation to determine where demonstrated competence supports operation; @sec-evaluation-trial-limits develops the limits of that evidence.

[^fn-ai-moravec-paradox]: **Moravec's Paradox**\index{Moravec's Paradox}: The observation in artificial intelligence [@moravec1988mind] that high-level reasoning requires comparatively little computation, whereas low-level sensorimotor coordination demands enormous perceptual and computational resources.

When a machine acts, it changes the conditions of its next observation. This is the feedback perspective associated with cybernetics[^fn-boundary-wiener-feedback] [@wiener1948cybernetics]. The warehouse robot's movement changes both its distance from the worker and the next image available to its model.

[^fn-boundary-wiener-feedback]: **Cybernetic Feedback Loops**\index{Cybernetic Feedback Loops}: In Norbert Wiener's cybernetic framework [@wiener1948cybernetics], feedback denotes adjusting future action using past performance.

Building the complete loop requires contributions from several disciplines. Machine learning supplies perception and action proposals. Computer systems determine how quickly the computation and communication finish, including the limits imposed by memory traffic [@williams2009roofline]. Mechanics and control establish which motions the plant can sustain. Embedded systems enforce the timing and access rules that connect a proposal to an actuator. These responsibilities meet at a common decision: whether the proposed action can execute under the machine's current conditions. This book develops the reasoning needed to make and justify that decision.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ The separation of learned proposals from actuation authority is mapped to isolated silicon domains in @sec-nervous-silicon-partitioning.
:::

{{< pagebreak >}}

::: {#dfn-boundary-physical-artificial-intelligence-physical-ai .callout-definition title="Physical artificial intelligence"}

***Physical artificial intelligence***\index{Physical Artificial Intelligence!definition}\index{Physical AI!definition} is the engineering of closed-loop machines in which learned models influence physical actions that change subsequent observations.

1.  **Significance**: Model performance becomes a property of an operating machine. Its actions must fit the plant's physical limits and the time available to respond.
2.  **Distinction**: The scope test later in this chapter combines a learned model, consequential physical feedback, and delegated physical authority. Neither a model used only for advice nor an automated machine without a learned component meets all three criteria.
3.  **Common pitfall**: Treating the body as a peripheral device for a model. A useful proposal still needs an independent permission decision based on the current state, physical limits, and available fallback.

:::

The first engineering distinction is between a proposed action and its physical effect. A short stopping calculation makes the cost of delay concrete. The scope test and machine model then organize the responsibilities needed to build the warehouse machine; the book's four parts develop them in detail.

## Defining the Cyber-Physical Causal Boundary {#sec-boundary-causal-boundary}

An advisory model that displays an inference result on a screen or returns a JSON payload to a web client has no direct electrical or mechanical coupling to physical actuators. A human operator may inspect and discard the prediction, or downstream business logic may reject a candidate token before committing an external transaction.[^fn-math-idempotency-physical] Neither property makes digital errors benign: an operator may act on flawed recommendations, and an automated algorithmic trading engine may execute catastrophic financial transactions across electronic exchanges. The relevant distinction is whether the automated system can turn an accepted model proposal into physical action. Arbitration belongs inside that system; it protects the causal boundary rather than removing it.

[^fn-math-idempotency-physical]: **Idempotency**\index{Idempotency}: Repeating an idempotent operation has the same specified result as executing it once. A motor setpoint command can have idempotent command semantics, but repeated execution may still dissipate energy. Idempotency does not imply reversibility or harmlessness.

### From a proposed action to motion {#sec-boundary-tensors-to-silicon}

In modern computational frameworks, executing `action_chunk = policy(observation)` produces a floating-point tensor. The tensor describes a proposed action; moving the machine requires a chain of controllers and physical actuators. The causal boundary is the interface through which an admitted command changes the physical plant.

A learned policy can propose a sequence of future positions or velocities. Those numbers remain a description of motion until a controller accepts and executes them. The representation and useful duration of such sequences are developed in @sec-brain; here the distinction is between describing an action and authorizing its consequences.

The permission path checks whether the proposed motion fits the current physical limits and can be carried out in time. If admitted, its setpoints pass to the controllers that drive the motors. A position controller determines the motion correction needed; the drive regulates electrical current to produce torque. @Sec-body develops the physical limits of this conversion, and @sec-nervous develops its timing and authority boundaries.

For a motor driven by pulse-width modulation (PWM), a software write sets a hardware timer's switching command. The power electronics use that signal to control current in the motor windings. Electromagnetic torque then accelerates the rotor and attached mechanism. This example establishes the distinction needed here: changing a proposed setpoint in memory is different from changing a command that has already produced motion. A later command can brake or redirect the machine, but that response takes time and must itself remain physically feasible.

::: {#dfn-boundary-causal-boundary .callout-definition title="Causal boundary"}

***Causal boundary***\index{Causal boundary!definition} is the interface through which a digital command produces physical forces, currents, or flows.

1.  **Significance**: A proposal can be rejected before it changes the plant. Once executed, it can alter the environment, dissipate energy, and change subsequent observations.
2.  **Distinction**: Restoring a command in memory does not restore the machine's prior physical state. Recovery requires another physical action, with its own limits and consequences.
3.  **Common pitfall**: Assuming that canceling a software task stops the motion it initiated. The machine needs a feasible stopping or holding response even when its proposer stops computing.

:::

An offline test can hold its examples fixed regardless of the model's predictions. A robot cannot generally rely on that separation: turning the chassis changes the next camera view, and pushing an object changes its location. The learning problem must account for observations that depend on earlier actions.

In a physical system, the environment evolves in a closed causal loop: the next physical state $\mathbf{s}_{t+1}$ and incoming sensor observation $\mathbf{o}_{t+1}$ depend directly on the action $\mathbf{a}_t$ produced by the prior model inference. The sensory input stream is endogenous, governed by closed-loop dynamics, represented here at successive observation times:
$$\mathbf{s}_{t+1} = \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{s}_t, \mathbf{a}_t), \quad \mathbf{o}_{t+1} \sim p(\mathbf{o} \mid \mathbf{s}_{t+1})$$

An erroneous action can therefore move the machine into states poorly represented in its training data. Errors in those states may produce further departures from the demonstrated behavior (@fig-01-causal-loop). This possibility motivates closed-loop evaluation; it does not mean that every error necessarily produces an unstable trajectory.

::: {#fig-01-causal-loop fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**The closed causal loop**: Advisory output (top) stops at an informational interface. In physical AI (bottom), permitted model proposals reach hardware registers, where electrical current produces force and motion. Those actions alter the environment and subsequent sensor observations." fig-alt="Flowchart contrasting advisory predictions with physical AI. The upper path ends at an informational interface; the lower path carries sensor observations to a proposal, the permission path, motor actuators, and a changing physical plant."}
![](images/svg/fig01_causal_loop.svg){width="95%"}
:::

### Delay consumes stopping clearance {#sec-boundary-kinematic-roofline}

A moving base needs distance both before braking begins and while braking brings it to rest. For a steady initial speed, constant deceleration after onset, and a stationary obstacle, the elementary stopping budget is:
$$d_{\text{stop}} = \underbrace{v \tau_{\text{delay}}}_{\text{computational blind travel}} + \underbrace{\frac{v^2}{2 a_{\max}}}_{\text{mechanical dissipation}} \le R_{\text{sensor}}$$
Here $v$ is the initial speed, $\tau_{\text{delay}}$ is the full interval from the relevant observation to the onset of retarding force, $a_{\max}$ is the braking deceleration assumed for this calculation, and $R_{\text{sensor}}$ is the usable observed clearance. The first term is travel during the delay; the second is travel while shedding kinetic energy. This simple bound is the starting point for the kinematic roofline, the speed limit imposed by available clearance and response time.

```{python}
#| label: boundary-blind-travel
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ BLIND TRAVEL OF THE RUNNING MACHINE (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: The blind-travel paragraph in @sec-boundary-causal-boundary.
# │ Goal: Convert the running machine's total pre-brake delay into distance.
# │ Show: Drive limit, total pre-brake delay, and travel before braking begins.
# │ How: v * tau_delay from the warehouse mobile manipulator and its aisle
# │      scenario in mlsysim; no value is retyped here.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_length, fmt_latency, fmt_velocity, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class BlindTravel:
    """Travel of the running machine's base before braking begins (illustrative inputs)."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    v = RM.base.max_velocity  # category: illustrative (drive limit)
    tau_delay = AISLE.tau_delay  # category: derived (capture to retarding force)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    blind = (v * tau_delay).to(millimeter)
    blind_display = round(blind.to(millimeter).magnitude) * millimeter

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(v.to(meter / second).magnitude - 1.5) < 1e-9, f"Canon drive limit is 1.5 m/s, got {v}.")
    check(abs(tau_delay.to(millisecond).magnitude - 133.6) < 5e-3, f"Canon tau_delay is 133.6 ms, got {tau_delay}.")
    check(abs(blind.to(millimeter).magnitude - 200.4) < 5e-3, f"Canon blind travel is 200 mm, got {blind}.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    v_str = fmt_velocity(v, unit=meter / second, precision=1)
    tau_delay_str = fmt_latency(tau_delay, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    blind_str = fmt_length(blind_display, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
```

```{python}
#| label: boundary-class1-momentum
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ MOMENTUM OF THE LOADED RUNNING MACHINE (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: The Class 1 worked paragraph in @sec-boundary-three-classes.
# │ Goal: Show what the loaded base carries at its drive limit and how the
# │       blind travel of the pre-brake delay compares with braking itself.
# │ Show: Loaded mass, kinetic energy, braking distance, and the blind travel
# │       as a share of the braking distance.
# │ How: calc_kinetic_energy and v^2/(2 a_brake) from the warehouse mobile
# │      manipulator and its aisle scenario in mlsysim; no value is retyped.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_length, fmt_energy, fmt_mass, fmt_velocity, fmt_acceleration, fmt_percent, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class MachineMomentum:
    """Energy and braking distance of the loaded base at its drive limit (illustrative inputs)."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    m_loaded = RM.loaded_mass  # category: derived (upper bound: base, arm, full tote rack)
    v = RM.base.max_velocity  # category: illustrative (drive limit)
    a_brake = AISLE.a_brake  # category: illustrative (credible deceleration, loaded, dry floor)
    tau_delay = AISLE.tau_delay  # category: derived (capture to retarding force)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    e_kinetic = calc_kinetic_energy(m_loaded, v).to(joule)
    d_brake = (v**2 / (2 * a_brake)).to(millimeter)
    blind = (v * tau_delay).to(millimeter)
    blind_share = (blind / d_brake).to("dimensionless").magnitude
    blind_display = round(blind.to(millimeter).magnitude) * millimeter

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(m_loaded.to(kilogram).magnitude - 368.0) < 1e-9, f"Canon loaded mass is 368 kg, got {m_loaded}.")
    check(abs(e_kinetic.to(joule).magnitude - 414.0) < 1e-9, f"Canon kinetic energy is 414 J, got {e_kinetic}.")
    check(abs(d_brake.to(millimeter).magnitude - 562.5) < 1e-9, f"Canon braking distance is 562.5 mm, got {d_brake}.")
    check(abs(blind_share - 0.356) < 5e-4, f"Blind travel is about 35.6 percent of braking, got {blind_share}.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    _m_loaded_str = fmt_mass(m_loaded, unit=kilogram, precision=0)
    v_str = fmt_velocity(v, unit=meter / second, precision=1)
    a_brake_str = fmt_acceleration(a_brake, unit=meter / second**2)
    _e_kinetic_str = fmt_energy(e_kinetic, unit=joule, precision=0)
    d_brake_str = fmt_length(d_brake, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    blind_str = fmt_length(blind_display, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    blind_share_str = fmt_percent(blind_share, precision=1, style="prose")
```

For the illustrative warehouse base, take a cruising speed of `{python} MachineMomentum.v_str`, a total pre-brake delay of `{python} BlindTravel.tau_delay_str`, and a credible deceleration of `{python} MachineMomentum.a_brake_str` under the scenario's loaded, dry-floor assumptions. Multiplying speed by delay gives `{python} BlindTravel.blind_str` of travel before braking begins. Braking then needs another `{python} MachineMomentum.d_brake_str`. The delay therefore adds `{python} MachineMomentum.blind_share_str` to the braking distance. These are chosen scenario inputs and derived distances, not measured stopping performance.

We can change that result through several engineering decisions. Reducing response delay reduces the first term; reducing speed reduces both terms, with braking distance falling quadratically. Selecting a model only for prediction accuracy misses this physical trade-off. Yet model execution time is not automatically the braking delay. An independent protective path can respond while the learned proposer is stalled, provided its own sensing, timing, power, and fallback remain valid. Its response path, rather than the stalled model's completion time, then determines the relevant delay.

The calculation is deliberately incomplete as a deployment bound. Acceleration before braking, uncertain traction, obstacles that move, tracking error, and the shape of the stopping trajectory require additional allowances. @Sec-body-kinetic-momentum establishes the physical budget, and later runtime design allocates the delays within it. The introductory result is already enough to change the design question from model accuracy alone to useful behavior delivered within a physical response budget.

### Irreversibility and recovery {#sec-boundary-thermodynamic-irreversibility}

A checkpoint can restore the logical state of a computation. It cannot restore a fixture already deformed by a gripper or remove heat already dissipated in a winding. A later command can brake, release, or redirect the machine, but that recovery takes time and must itself be physically feasible. Preventive checks and recovery therefore serve different purposes.

Stopping clearance makes irreversibility visible for the mobile base. When the same machine grasps an object or holds a load, contact force and sustained energy demand can become the limiting quantities. The architecture must account for the kind of physical work the task requires.

## Three Machine Classes {#sec-boundary-three-classes}

The warehouse machine changes its limiting problem as it works. While traveling down an aisle, it needs room to stop. While pressing a door latch, it must limit contact force. While holding a load, it must supply torque without exhausting its thermal or electrical margin. These operating constraints motivate the three machine classes in @fig-01-three-archetypes.

**Mass-dominated mobility** spends stopping clearance. A mobile base, delivery vehicle, or drone carries momentum and cannot stop instantaneously. Speed, response delay, and available braking or thrust determine the room needed to change its motion.

**Contact-dominated manipulation** spends force and deformation margin. A gripper pressing against a stiff fixture can build damaging force while moving only a short distance. The useful action is still contact: opening the latch requires force. The engineering task is to deliver enough force for the task while respecting the object and mechanism's limits.

**Energy- and thermal-dominated operation** spends heat and supply margins. Holding a payload may require sustained motor current even when nothing moves. A simultaneous demand from drives and computation can also reduce the shared supply voltage. The machine must sustain the work long enough to complete its mission and preserve the resources required for its protective response.

::: {#fig-01-three-archetypes fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Three machine classes**: The three foundational physical embodiments classified by their primary binding conservation laws: (a) mass-dominated mobility (Class 1) governed by momentum and spatial clearance; (b) contact-dominated manipulation (Class 2) governed by mechanical impedance and structural yield stress; and (c) energy- and thermal-dominated dynamics (Class 3) governed by thermal capacitance, Joule heating, and power delivery." fig-alt="Three machine classes of physical AI classified by binding conservation laws: mass-dominated mobility governed by momentum and stopping clearance, contact-dominated manipulation governed by mechanical impedance and structural yield stress, and energy-dominated systems governed by thermal capacitance and power delivery."}
![](images/svg/fig01_three_archetypes.svg){width="100%"}
:::

The classes identify a dominant constraint, not mutually exclusive kinds of robot. Our mobile manipulator has a wheeled base, an articulated arm, navigation sensors, and a wrist camera. A learned policy can coordinate base and arm proposals [@fu2024mobile], while the assembled machine must respect all applicable limits. A fixed arm also has thermal and electrical constraints; a mobile base also encounters contact.

::: {#capstone-boundary-humanoid-crucible .callout-perspective title="The humanoid crucible"}
A humanoid makes the coupling especially visible. Catching a load perturbs balance, a recovery step demands additional torque, and that torque draws current and generates heat. Protecting the control electronics does not by itself supply the drive energy needed for the recovery. The part-ending humanoid examples test how each engineering principle survives these coupled demands.
:::

The first design task is to identify which margin the intended action approaches, then establish the physical response available before that margin is exhausted. The detailed force, heat, and power calculations belong to the body's design. A separate scope test determines whether the machine also needs the learning and delegated-authority discipline developed in this book.

## The Physical AI Scope Test {#sec-boundary-scope-test}

A warehouse arm can follow a fixed control law, execute a human-approved offline path, or accept live learned proposals. All three can move the same hardware, but they place different obligations on the system. The scope test identifies the combination developed in this book.

The scope of physical AI is defined by the simultaneous intersection of three structural criteria (@fig-01-scope-venn):

1. **Learned Statistical Model:** The system relies on a policy, perception encoder, or world model acquired from data, such as a neural network or diffusion policy [@chi2024diffusionpolicy]. The criterion concerns how the component is obtained and used, not its size or whether its outputs can be bounded mathematically. Its learned behavior contributes to the actions the system proposes.
2. **Consequential Physical Feedback:** Actuator actions alter the material state of the physical environment, which in turn directly dictates what the sensors observe next under the governing laws of classical mechanics, thermodynamics, or electromagnetism.
3. **Delegated Physical Authority (System-Level Actuation):** A learned component supplies live proposals that an automated system can execute without synchronous human approval. The learned model need not write an actuator register itself; the system holds physical authority because an accepted proposal can reach one.

::: {#fig-01-scope-venn fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**The physical AI scope test**: Physical AI combines a learned component, consequential physical feedback, and system-level authority to execute accepted proposals without human approval. An independent veto belongs inside this intersection because accepted proposals can still move the plant. The pairwise overlaps locate advisory systems, digital autonomy, and classical control." fig-alt="Three-set Venn diagram defining physical AI at the intersection of learned models, physical feedback, and physical authority. The pairwise overlaps show advisory systems, digital autonomy, and classical control."}
![](images/svg/fig01_scope_venn.svg){width="90%"}
:::

A classical proportional-integral-derivative (PID) controller can regulate a motor through physical feedback without a learned component. Conversely, a learned market predictor can influence automated transactions without controlling the physical plant considered here. Neither satisfies all three criteria. This distinction identifies the engineering scope; it does not imply that either system is simple or harmless.

A learned model alone cannot define the field. An offline neural trajectory optimizer may compute paths for a manipulator, but if an engineer must inspect and explicitly load each path before execution, its outputs lack delegated runtime authority. A model that flags assembly defects on a display likewise leaves the physical decision to another actor.

Shared autonomy belongs inside the scope whenever a learned component can affect live motion without approval of each correction. A surgical assistant that applies learned haptic guidance can influence contact before the surgeon responds, even though the surgeon remains responsible for the overall task. No universal force threshold or human reaction time determines this classification. What matters is whether the automated system can execute the learned contribution.

Evaluating an ambiguous machine means testing each criterion independently, as the examples above do. A deterministic veto does not remove delegated authority; a mandatory human review of an offline plan does. When all three tests pass, the system operates as physical AI, and its engineering must respect the causal boundary established in @sec-boundary-causal-boundary.

::: {#chk-boundary-scope-test .callout-checkpoint title="Binding budgets and the scope test"}

- [ ] Can you explain why response delay and active braking consume separate portions of stopping clearance?
- [ ] Can you identify the relevant physical margins when the warehouse machine travels, presses a latch, and holds a load?
- [ ] Can you apply all three scope criteria to a new machine, including one whose learned output passes through an independent veto?

:::

The scope test establishes which responsibilities must be combined. The machine model places those responsibilities along the path from observation to physical action.

## The Machine in Five Levels {#sec-boundary-machine-model}

A machine that passes the scope test needs an organization that keeps its learned models from writing directly to the actuators they could damage, while still letting those models steer it.

The Body establishes what motion, force, and power the machine can sustain. The Brain supplies learned proposals within those limits. The Nervous System connects the two while preserving the time and authority needed to refuse an inadmissible proposal. The five-level model locates these responsibilities from learned computation down to the physical environment:

1. **The Brain (Level 1):** The learned models that interpret observations and propose goals or motion. A proposed sequence of future setpoints does not establish permission to execute the entire sequence.
2. **The Nervous System (Level 2):** The communication and control mechanisms that connect proposals to execution. Its permission path admits, modifies, or refuses proposals using current evidence and physical limits, and can initiate a feasible fallback without waiting for the proposer.
3. **The Body (Level 3):** The drives, transmissions, windings, structures, and power supply that deliver the admitted action.
4. **The Boundary (Level 4):** The interface where commands produce physical effects and sensors convert physical events into measurements.
5. **The World (Level 5):** Floors, payloads, contact, people, and other conditions that continue evolving whether the machine observes them or not.

One implementation places the learned proposer on an application processor, the permission path on a separate real-time controller, and the motor current loops on dedicated drives. The required separation follows from timing and fault assumptions; naming a processor family or operating system does not establish it. @Sec-nervous turns this division of responsibility into an explicit handoff contract.

Governance is not a sixth level. It is the lifecycle envelope around all five, deciding who may command the machine, what evidence licenses it to operate, and when that license expires, and it changes on the timescale of interventions and releases rather than control cycles.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ Transfers of command authority, and preemption of the proposal stream, are governed by the supervisor state machine in @sec-intervention-authority-transitions.
:::

::: {#dfn-boundary-proposal-boundary .callout-definition title="Proposal boundary"}

***Proposal boundary***\index{Proposal boundary!definition}\index{Permission path!definition} is the line between a learned model, which may only propose an action, and the **permission path**, an independent mechanism with bounded latency that the model cannot delay or corrupt and that alone may permit the action to reach an actuator. The permission path checks each proposal against fresh evidence, the stopping envelope, and a fallback feasible from the current state, and refuses when any check fails.

1.  **Significance**: Keeps model outputs from directly commanding actuators; the protection holds only while the permission path's sensing, physical limits, and fallback remain valid.
2.  **Distinction**: A policy that outputs torque values still has no actuator-write authority; its output is a proposal until the permission path admits it.
3.  **Common pitfall**: Treating the permission path as a post-processing clamp on model outputs rather than an independent mechanism that can refuse execution when the proposer is late, wrong, or silent.

The proposal boundary governs who may authorize an action. The causal boundary is where the admitted command changes the plant. The Nervous System connects the two, checking proposals before allowing the drives to execute them.

:::

The margin stack that opens every chapter draws these same five levels (@fig-01-locator). The rates shown in the locator belong to the book's selected architecture; they are not universal requirements for each level. Later chapters derive the necessary timing from the task and body. For orientation, the essential feature is the proposal boundary between learned computation and execution authority.

::: {#fig-01-locator fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**The five-level machine**: Each band carries its pinned rate and the chapters that work on it. The wider gap between Brain and Nervous System marks the proposal boundary, above which a component may only propose. A chapter-opening stack with no level highlighted marks a governance chapter. A useful machine needs both capable proposals and a dependable execution path. The separation does not require refusing every imperfect proposal; a permitted correction can preserve task success while enforcing a physical limit. Performance evaluation must distinguish what the learned proposer accomplishes alone, what the whole machine accomplishes with normal corrections, and whether the protective response contains a hazard.

These responsibilities define the questions carried through the book. They also provide a way to analyze a failure without attributing every outcome to model accuracy.

## The Four Bedrock Laws {#sec-boundary-bedrock-laws}

Opening a door and carrying a load require more than a sequence of accurate predictions. The machine must respect its body's limits, learn from experience changed by its own actions, and connect proposals to justified execution. Four bedrock laws organize these responsibilities, each leading a part of the book.

**The first law: irreversibility.** Software rollback cannot undo physical consequences. The checks needed to admit an action must finish before that action consumes the available margin. The stopping calculation already showed why: delay spends clearance, and braking then needs additional distance. Reversing a command may recover a position, but it cannot repair a damaged object or erase heat already dissipated. Part I turns this distinction into physical budgets for the body and timing requirements for its controllers.

**The second law: endogenous data.** A physical agent's actions influence its future observations. A grasp changes the object's pose, and a poor approach can move the machine into states absent from its demonstrations. Single-step prediction accuracy therefore does not establish closed-loop competence. Part II develops collection, training, and evaluation as an improvement cycle: identify a failed behavior, gather suitable new experience, train a candidate, and test both its gains and regressions. Current evidence bounds the current claim; qualified new experience can expand it.

**The third law: proposal is not permission.** A learned model may propose; an independent permission path decides whether the proposal may execute. That decision requires sufficiently fresh state, applicable physical limits, and a feasible fallback when a proposal is late, absent, or inadmissible. Independence must hold under the stated timing and fault assumptions: the proposer must not be able to delay or corrupt the mechanism responsible for refusal. Part III builds the runtime around this separation of authority.

**The fourth law: evidence bounds authority.** Permission to operate depends on evidence for stated conditions. A successful demonstration does not establish safe behavior for every payload, sensor fault, or surface. The release argument must identify the supported operating domain, the assumptions behind its limits, and the conditions that require restricted operation or withdrawal. Part IV develops command authority, fault testing, and release decisions so that uncertainty limits what the machine is allowed to do.

The proposal boundary joins the four laws. Irreversibility requires checks before consequential action; endogenous data limits what training alone establishes; and evidence bounds the conditions under which admission is justified. More capable models do not remove these obligations. General methods can benefit from increased computation [@sutton2019bitter], but onboard computation still consumes memory bandwidth, energy, and cooling capacity. This book calls those constraints the **physical wall**\index{Physical Wall}; @sec-brain-cognitive-pipeline measures their effect on the proposers. A refusal must also have a physical meaning: terminating computation does not stop a moving machine, so the runtime needs a timely response that the body can execute.

## The Architecture of This Book {#sec-boundary-book-architecture}

The book develops the ability to carry a learned proposal from a physical requirement to justified operation. The engineer first bounds what the machine can do, then establishes what its learned proposer has demonstrated, builds the runtime that checks live proposals, and tests the conditions under which operation may continue. Each part is led by one of the four laws. The records in @fig-01-spine preserve the assumptions and results of this reasoning so that later decisions can use them. One strand carries physical limits and evidence of competence; another carries the current observation and proposed action. They meet at the permission decision. @Sec-frontier-architectural-synthesis returns to the resulting engineering capability and the premises on which each claim depends.

::: {#fig-01-spine fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**The spine of the book**: Each part is led by one law, and each chapter of Parts I to IV except @sec-brain produces a record that a later one consumes. What the plant can do and what the proposer has shown it can do run as one strand, what the proposer proposes now as another, and the two meet at the permission decision." fig-alt="Flow diagram of fifteen record boxes, each labeled with its chapter number, on shaded bands for the four parts. A label at top left reads Chapter 1, What must be guaranteed. In the Part I band, labeled Irreversibility, the limit record of Chapter 2 feeds the handoff record of Chapter 4, and a dashed arrow labeled Chapter 3, proposer limits, also enters the handoff record. The handoff record forks into two rows. The upper row, in the Part II band labeled Endogenous data, runs provenance record 5, policy manifest 6, and evaluation record 7. The lower row, in the Part III band labeled Proposal is not permission, runs observation contract 8, belief record 9, intent lease 10, and trajectory record 11. Both rows converge on the enforcement record of Chapter 12, which feeds the placement record of Chapter 13. An arrow then runs down to a lower row in the Part IV band, labeled Evidence bounds authority: authority record 14, fault record 15, and release manifest 16, which feeds the residual-claims register of Chapter 17, labeled Conclusion and What the evidence supports. A separate arrow runs from the evaluation record around the top and right edges to the release manifest."}
![](images/svg/fig01_book_spine.svg){width="100%"}
:::

Part I, The Machine Anatomy, turns irreversibility into design limits. @Sec-body measures the plant's budgets, @sec-brain establishes what the learned proposer can supply on time, and @sec-nervous connects them through a permission path whose timing follows from those budgets. The limit and handoff records make those assumptions explicit. Part II, Teaching the Machine, follows the consequences of actions changing future observations. @Sec-data, @sec-training, and @sec-evaluation develop the evidence needed to collect demonstrations, train a policy, and assess its competence within a declared operating domain. The provenance record, policy manifest, and evaluation record preserve both the supported claims and their gaps.

Part III, Running the Machine, implements the distinction between proposing and permitting an action. @Sec-perception through @sec-placement follow a command from a timestamped observation through a belief, an intent lease, and a proposed trajectory to admission and timely execution. Part IV, Governing the Machine, determines how evidence limits continued operation. @Sec-intervention, @sec-verification, and @sec-release address command authority, fault tests, and release conditions. @Sec-frontier concludes by applying the method to an unfamiliar machine, synthesizing what an engineer can now build and justify, and identifying the work needed to extend that capability. Across these parts, the warehouse mobile manipulator introduced here gives the reader one machine on which to connect the decisions. Its records make the reasoning inspectable; completing a record does not establish that the machine satisfies the physical claim it contains.

The route is a method for making useful behavior dependable. A documented failure now illustrates why these responsibilities must be joined before a machine enters service.

## When the Responsibilities Fail Together {#sec-boundary-when-fails}

A warehouse model that recognizes an obstacle too late cannot recover the clearance already consumed. In a road vehicle, the same timing problem can combine with tracking errors, delayed intervention, and missing redundancy. The 2018 Tempe collision provides a documented example of these interacting failures; it does not establish that one prescribed hardware architecture would have prevented them.

On a March night in 2018, a modified Volvo XC90 operating Uber Advanced Technologies Group's developmental automated driving system (ADS) struck and fatally injured a pedestrian pushing a bicycle across a road in Tempe, Arizona [@ntsb2019uber].[^fn-inc-tempe-investigation] The vehicle carried lidar, radar, and cameras (@fig-01-tempe-vehicle). The ADS first detected the pedestrian $5.6\text{ s}$ before impact, but detection alone did not provide a correct path prediction [@ntsb2019uber].

[^fn-inc-tempe-investigation]: **2018 Tempe Autonomous Collision**\index{2018 Tempe Autonomous Collision!NTSB report}: The event times and design details in this section come from NTSB highway accident report NTSB/HAR-19/03 [@ntsb2019uber].

### Tracking history loss under classification churn {#sec-boundary-tracking-churn}

Despite continuing to track the detected object, the ADS did not brake in response to it. The NTSB record shows classification changes among vehicle, bicycle, and other before $T-1.2\text{ s}$ [@ntsb2019uber].

When the classification changed, the ADS path predictor did not use the object's earlier locations; for an "other" object it could assume a static path.[^fn-ctrl-kalman-tracking] The loss of earlier locations matters because successive positions provide evidence of motion across the roadway. A changing semantic label must not silently discard that evidence. The resulting path predictions did not place the pedestrian in the SUV's lane until $T-1.2\text{ s}$ [@ntsb2019uber].

[^fn-ctrl-kalman-tracking]: **Tracking History**\index{Tracking history!classification changes}: A path predictor can estimate motion from successive object locations. In the Tempe ADS, a changed classification caused the predictor to omit earlier locations; the NTSB report does not specify a Kalman-filter reset or a zero-velocity initialization [@ntsb2019uber].

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ The stopping envelopes in @sec-enforcement-stopping-envelopes bound what a classification change like Tempe's can cost.
:::

### Action suppression and the kinematic stopping deficit {#sec-boundary-action-suppression}

The ADS included an action-suppression interval intended to reduce responses to false alarms while the system checked the situation and allowed operator intervention [@ntsb2019uber]. That software choice also consumed time available for a physical response.

At $T-1.2\text{ s}$, with the vehicle traveling at $43.2\text{ mph}$, the ADS recognized an emergency and entered its one-second action-suppression period. The design withheld braking while it checked the hazard or waited for operator intervention. At $T-0.2\text{ s}$, suppression ended. The ADS then initiated a plan for gradual slowdown and sounded an alert; it did not request emergency braking. The NTSB notes that communication delay leaves unclear whether that slowdown began before the operator disengaged the ADS at $T-0.02\text{ s}$ [@ntsb2019uber].

The warehouse calculation explains the consequence without reconstructing the crash. Travel during a withheld response leaves less clearance for braking afterward. Detection, correct path prediction, hazard recognition, and physical braking are distinct events; reporting the first detection time alone conceals the failures between them.

::: {#fig-01-tempe-vehicle fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Tempe test vehicle sensor locations**: The NTSB diagram identifies the developmental ADS vehicle's lidar, camera, radar, computing, and telecommunications locations. (Source: NTSB, public domain)." fig-alt="NTSB side-view diagram of the Volvo test vehicle with colored outlines marking lidar, cameras, radar, ADS computing and data storage, and GPS equipment."}
![](images/jpg/fig01_real_ntsb_tempe_vehicle.jpg){width="95%"}
:::

::: {#ws-boundary-missing-safety-referee .callout-war-story title="The disabled safety redundancy (2018)"}
**Context**: On March 18, 2018, a developmental ADS on a 2017 Volvo XC90 struck and killed a pedestrian crossing a road in Tempe, Arizona [@ntsb2019uber].

**Mechanism**: As traced above, classification changes discarded the object's tracking history, and the one-second suppression withheld braking until only a gradual slowdown was planned. The design did not use maximum braking solely to mitigate an unavoidable collision [@ntsb2019uber].

**Impact**: The vehicle struck and fatally injured the pedestrian. The late gradual-slowdown plan could not recover the lost stopping opportunity.

**Response**: The NTSB found that disabling the Volvo warning and braking systems, which Uber ATG had done over possible radar interference, removed a safety redundancy layer and recommended stronger safety risk management for testing automated vehicles [@ntsb2019uber].

**Systems lesson**: Classification uncertainty, a delayed response rule, and reliance on an inattentive operator can combine. A design needs timely hazard assessment and a response that can mitigate impact when avoidance is no longer possible; the investigation does not prescribe a particular processor or mailbox architecture.
:::

The investigation supports a broader architectural requirement. A developmental ADS needs safety redundancy and a timely mitigation path even when perception or path prediction fails, and simulation tests by Volvo that the NTSB cites suggest that the factory emergency braking might have prevented or mitigated this collision. The report does not establish when a separate permission path would have triggered or where it would have stopped the vehicle.[^fn-std-safety-standards]

[^fn-std-safety-standards]: **Safety-Critical Standards**\index{Safety-Critical Standards!autonomous systems}: Functional safety and intended-functionality standards can inform the safety case for sensing, actuation, and fallback. Their applicability and required implementation depend on the system and jurisdiction; the NTSB Tempe report did not mandate an isolated microcontroller architecture.

Tempe illustrates failure *before* impact, where classification changes and a software suppression delay prevented timely braking. The 2023 Cruise robotaxi incident [@quinnemanuel2024cruise] marks the opposite pole *after* impact, a post-collision fallback that moved the vehicle while a pedestrian was pinned beneath it (@sec-enforcement-fallback-ladder).

Neither failure reduces to an inaccurate model. The first spent stopping distance before braking began, and no later action could recover it. The second chose motion after the impact. Together they show what must hold before the machine acts and what a fallback may do once harm has begun, and connect the four laws to decisions made across an entire system.

::: {#chk-boundary-forensic-failure .callout-checkpoint title="Forensics of boundary and authority failures"}

Verify how the Tempe mechanisms connect to the architecture:

- [ ] **Classification changes and path prediction**: Can you explain how classification changes caused the ADS path predictor to omit earlier object locations, despite continued tracking?
- [ ] **Software suppression vs. kinematic clearance**: Can you distinguish the $T-1.2\text{ s}$ recognition time from the one-second suppression period and explain why the gradual-slowdown plan at $T-0.2\text{ s}$ could not restore the time already spent?
- [ ] **Safety redundancy**: Can you explain why disabling factory collision warning and emergency braking removed a layer of protection from a developmental ADS?

:::

## Safety Convergence {#sec-boundary-safety-convergence}

A robot approaching the end of an aisle needs a valid stopping decision whether its camera is dirty, its observations have been manipulated, or its model has made an ordinary prediction error. Safety concerns the resulting physical harm; security concerns deliberate interference; accountability concerns the evidence needed to explain the decision. These responsibilities intersect where the system authorizes motion.

For an ordinary failure, consider traction falling below the value assumed in the stopping calculation. The previous clearance bound may no longer support the same speed. Detecting that change and restricting operation requires evidence about the plant and environment, not merely confidence in the model's proposed path.

An adversary can instead target the evidence used to authorize motion. Corrupted observations or unauthorized command changes can alter a physical decision even when the model runs correctly. Independence from the proposer alone does not establish trustworthy sensing or authorized requests.

A valid credential establishes who may request an action, but not whether that action is physically admissible now. The same joint command can be acceptable far from a hard stop and inadmissible near it. **Physical authority is state-dependent.** Admission must consider current motion, load, temperature, and uncertainty, together with a response that remains feasible if operation cannot continue.

Accountability requires records that connect the decision to its physical outcome. The engineer needs to reconstruct the proposal, the state estimate and limits used to judge it, the admitted command, and the observed response. The records also need timing information precise enough to establish which evidence was available when the decision occurred. Recording a command does not prove that the actuator executed it, so command and feedback evidence serve different roles. Later chapters develop these records alongside the mechanisms they describe.

Safety, security, and accountability therefore ask the same three things of the permission path that guards the causal boundary: state fresh enough to judge the command, authority to refuse it, and a record of what was proposed, what was admitted, and what was written. This path supports a larger engineering task: choosing a useful physical capability, developing the learned behavior that supplies it, and integrating a machine that can deliver it under justified operating conditions.

## Fallacies and Pitfalls {#sec-boundary-fallacies-pitfalls}

Each misconception below imports an assumption that holds for software, for offline learning, or for classical control into a machine whose learned proposals can reach an actuator. The first assumes that training can do the permission path's work, and the other three assume that a human can intervene instantly, that latency only degrades performance, or that physical work can be undone.

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Fallacy**: *Safety constraints can be trained into the policy.*

Learning pipelines often try to make a policy safe by penalizing undesirable behavior during training. Such objectives can reduce undesirable behavior on the training distribution, but that alone does not establish a bound on every command the deployed policy emits. Under novel sensor noise, a lens occlusion, or an out-of-distribution combination of states, nothing in the offline objective prevents an unsafe command. A training incentive shapes a probability distribution, whereas a stopping envelope requires a bound that holds on every cycle. The constraint therefore belongs downstream of the model, as a gate between the policy output and the actuator registers, which is where the third law places the permission path.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Pitfall**: *Treating human supervisory intervention as instantaneous in shared-autonomy systems.*

A surgical tool applies haptic guidance force feedback from a learned anatomical model while a surgeon holds the instrument. Human supervision does not remove delegated authority during the interval before the surgeon can respond. If an actuator builds force before the operator can respond, its commands can deform tissue before the operator corrects them. The engineering question is how much force the system can apply during that interval. Local force limits enforced by the permission path must constrain the actuator without depending on either a timely neural prediction or an immediate human response.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Pitfall**: *Assuming software latency merely degrades performance gracefully.*

A stalled proposer becomes dangerous if its last command remains active beyond the conditions supporting it. Execution therefore needs a bounded lifetime and a feasible response when that lifetime ends. Refusing an invalid replacement need not cancel an active command that remains valid, but it cannot extend that command's authority. An independent permission path can make a proposer stall a loss of availability rather than a loss of protection, only while its own evidence, timing, power, and fallback premises hold.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Fallacy**: *Assuming physical actuation is reversible through subsequent software compensation.*

A manipulator applies excessive torque to a delicate fixture. Its monitor detects the anomaly after contact and reverses the motor command. Reversing a command cannot restore a fixture that has already plastically deformed or recover the energy already dissipated as physical heat in the motor windings ($I^2 R$). Detection can limit further damage, but it cannot erase the intervening physical work. The control architecture must therefore check commands against force and motion limits before execution. Recovery remains necessary, but it complements preventive enforcement rather than replacing it.

:::

## Summary {#sec-boundary-summary}

The causal boundary connects an admitted command to a physical effect. Restoring a software state cannot undo that effect; recovery requires another feasible physical response. A moving machine also travels while computation proceeds, so the chapter's timing and authority requirements place admission checks before consequential action. The warehouse example and the Tempe analysis show why prediction quality must be considered together with response time and available stopping clearance.

::: {.callout-takeaways title="Engineering across the causal boundary"}
* **Useful behavior needs a complete machine**: Physical AI combines learned behavior, consequential physical feedback, and delegated authority. Designing it requires connecting task competence to the body, runtime, and evidence supporting operation.
* **Response delay spends physical margin**: In the illustrative warehouse calculation, pre-brake travel adds `{python} MachineMomentum.blind_share_str` to braking distance. The relevant delay belongs to the path that produces the response, which can be independent of the learned proposer's completion time.
* **Proposal and permission have different jobs**: The Brain proposes useful actions; the permission path admits, modifies, or refuses them under current conditions. Its protection depends on valid evidence, physical limits, timing, and a feasible fallback.
* **Evidence guides improvement and operation**: The four parts connect machine anatomy, learning, execution, and governance. Their purpose is both to establish useful service under stated conditions and to identify the experiments or design changes needed to extend it.
:::

The engineer's task is to make the machine perform a useful physical task within its limits. That requires learned behavior suited to the task, timely computation, and a body able to deliver the requested motion. An independent permission path constrains execution even when the proposer is unavailable, subject to valid sensing, physical limits, and a feasible fallback. The next step is to establish those limits for the body that will carry out the action.

::: {.callout-chapter-connection title="From the causal boundary to physical limits"}
A permission decision needs a physical limit against which to judge the proposed action. @Sec-body begins Part I by deriving stopping, actuator, thermal, and electrical budgets and examining how to measure them under stated operating conditions. Those measurements enter the limit record. @Sec-brain then examines the learned proposer's capabilities and timing, and @sec-nervous uses both sets of constraints to design the handoff and independent permission path. The progression starts with what the machine can sustain and ends with how computation may safely request it.
:::
